summary: Examines how Remote Direct Memory Access could help NFS, which has historically had high overhead from copying data on end hosts. It explores potential benefits and the problems to solve.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally moving a file means copying it several times inside the computer. This note asks whether the network card could drop data straight into memory, making file sharing faster.

subtitle: How network file sharing becomes too slow when data must be copied many times.

tldr.problem: NFS (Network File System) suffers from high CPU overhead because data must be copied many times as it moves from the network into application memory, between kernel buffers, during data format conversion, and back again. At speeds above 1 Gbps, this copying becomes the main bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) lets the network interface card write data directly into application memory, bypassing the CPU and kernel copies. By separating control information (sent inline) from data chunks (transferred via RDMA), NFS can achieve file access performance approaching that of local disks.
tldr.outcome: RDMA-based NFS can reach theoretical network throughput while using less than half the CPU of conventional NFS, enabling high-performance network storage for databases, clusters, and enterprise storage.

facts.label: RDMA NFS CPU at full throughput

today: This problem statement motivated the development of NFS over RDMA (specified in later RFCs), which enables high-performance network storage for enterprise and cloud infrastructure, databases, and scientific computing systems. The principles described here apply to any data-intensive network protocol.

sections.title: The NFS Performance Problem
sections.content:
NFS (Network File System) is the standard way Unix and Linux systems share files across a network. It is convenient and has been popular for decades. However, NFS has a serious performance problem.

Accessing a local disk is very fast because the storage controller reads data once and puts it directly into the application's memory. NFS must send that data over the network, then process it through multiple software layers: the network stack, the TCP/IP stack, the RPC (Remote Procedure Call) layer, the XDR (External Data Representation) encoding layer, kernel buffers, and finally into the application.

Each layer may copy the data, sometimes multiple times. Research shows that on modern systems, even with optimizations, NFS over a 1 Gigabit network hits a wall at around 60 MB/s—not because the network is slow, but because the CPU is busy copying data instead of doing real work.
sections.plainLanguage: When you download a file over the network, the computer copies it from the network card to a buffer, then to another buffer, then to another buffer, then to your program. By the time the data gets to your program, the computer has worked so hard copying that there is no time for anything else.

sections.title: Why Data Copying Costs So Much
sections.content:
Each data copy has a cost: it uses the system bus and CPU cache. Modern networks run at gigabit or higher speeds, but the system bus and memory bandwidth have not grown as fast. When a 10 Gigabit network card tries to push data through a system bus that was not designed for it, copying becomes the bottleneck.

The problem is worse in NFS because of how RPC and XDR work: data arrives at arbitrary byte alignment (not naturally aligned in memory), so it must be copied to aligned buffers. RPC request/response operations complete out of order, preventing simple pipeline optimizations. NFS version 4 added the COMPOUND operation and security information that further reduce alignment opportunities.

Attempts to avoid copies through clever buffer management or virtual memory tricks work for some cases but are fragile, version-specific, and hardware-dependent. None of them solve the fundamental problem: the CPU is the bottleneck, not the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer is fast, but moving data from place to place inside the computer is even slower than moving it over the network. The CPU spends all its time copying instead of processing.

sections.title: How RDMA Solves the Problem
sections.content:
RDMA stands for Remote Direct Memory Access. With RDMA, the network interface card can read from and write to application memory directly, without CPU intervention. The RPC layer separates control information (RPC headers, operation codes, small metadata) from bulk data.

Control information travels inline in the RPC message, processed normally by the CPU. Bulk data (file content, large metadata) is transferred via RDMA Write (server to client) or RDMA Read (client fetching from server) operations. Each bulk data chunk includes a "placement hint" telling the NIC exactly where in application memory to write or read the data.

The result: data moves once, directly from the network into the application's buffer. No intermediate copies, no kernel buffer, no XDR marshalling of the bulk payload. The CPU is free to do useful work.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of copying the data five times, the network card puts it straight where the program needs it. The computer just watches and tells the network card what to do.

sections.title: Measured Performance Improvements
sections.content:
Tests comparing conventional NFS to RDMA-based NFS over Gigabit Ethernet show dramatic results. With conventional NFS, throughput plateaus at 60 MB/s with the CPU saturated at 100% utilization across all file sizes.

Over RDMA, the same hardware achieves the theoretical maximum throughput of the platform (around 100 MB/s for the test hardware) at 256 KB block size while using only 100% CPU at that maximum throughput. Smaller reads (2 KB blocks) achieve 10 MB/s using only 45% CPU, and 16 KB reads achieve 40 MB/s at 70% CPU usage.

The improvement is even more dramatic at higher network speeds. For 10 Gigabit networks, conventional NFS cannot saturate the link due to CPU bottleneck, while RDMA-based NFS can approach line rate. This is critical for high-performance storage, database clusters, and cloud infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: With regular NFS, the computer can only do 60 megabytes per second because the CPU is exhausted copying. With RDMA, it can do twice as much while using less than half the CPU.

sections.title: Security and Integrity Protection
sections.content:
RDMA's performance benefits come with a challenge: security. NFS implementations typically rely on the RPC layer for authentication and integrity checking via RPCSEC_GSS. These mechanisms require the CPU to process each message locally, exactly the overhead RDMA is designed to avoid.

To maintain NFS security without sacrificing RDMA performance, the solution uses Channel Binding: delegate session integrity and privacy protection to the RDMA layer itself. The RDMA hardware can offload encryption and authentication, processing the data inline as it transfers it, without CPU intervention.

Additionally, RDMA must ensure that direct memory access cannot violate system security. RDMA providers must conform to security models that prevent access to memory outside the granted regions, protecting both the kernel and other user processes from unauthorized data access.
sections.plainLanguage: The network card checks that messages are trustworthy and correctly delivered, not the CPU. That way, the CPU is still free to do other things.
